prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

I can’t get rid of useful things and nobody wants to pick them up, I keep forgetting where I lay my umbrella. I don’t leave footprints in the snow anymore, we haven’t had a war on domestic soil in so long I wonder if I still got it. Because once I had it. I heard about a boy who once tied a string to his brother, he tied his brother to the ocean and the ocean to the blackbird— from the ground all the birds look like blackbirds from the ground a Stealth Bomber looks like a spaceship. The aliens are coming, they walk through birthday parties and basically go unnoticed. And this is kind of how I go through life, once I heated up a spoon in the microwave the fish have so much mercury in them they spark. I was handed a bayonet from the Civil War and a copper penny corroded with rust. When they take the Statue of Liberty apart to clean her her neck explodes with a million little spiders. Meanwhile in a forest somewhere someone cut open my grandmother’s belly and filled it with bricks something is coming soon I keep a bucket of lambs blood by the front door.

outputs.L1:
Here are two ways to polish your text, depending on the tone you wish to achieve. 

Because the original text is deeply evocative, surreal, and poetic, these options retain all of your original imagery and meaning while elevating the diction, structure, and flow.

### Option 1: Lyrical & Eloquent (Recommended)
*This version refines the grammar and cadence into a sophisticated, haunting piece of prose poetry.*

> "I am unable to part with useful things, yet no one comes to collect them. I repeatedly forget where I have laid my umbrella. I no longer leave footprints in the snow. It has been so long since war touched our domestic soil that I wonder if I still retain my edge—for I certainly possessed it once. 
> 
> I heard of a boy who tied a string to his brother, tethering him to the ocean, and the ocean to a blackbird. From the ground, all birds resemble blackbirds, just as a Stealth Bomber looks like a spaceship. The extraterrestrials are arriving; they drift through birthday parties virtually unnoticed. In much the same way, I move through life. 
> 
> Once, I heated a metal spoon in the microwave; now, the fish contain so much mercury that they spark. I was handed a bayonet from the Civil War alongside a copper penny corroded with age. When they dismantle the Statue of Liberty for cleaning, her neck erupts with a million tiny spiders. Meanwhile, in a distant forest, someone has cut open my grandmother’s belly and filled it with bricks. Something is approaching soon; I keep a bucket of lamb’s blood beside the front door."

---

### Option 2: Formal & Articulate
*This version organizes the stream-of-consciousness thoughts into clear, structured sentences, suitable for a formal narrative or essay.*

> "I find myself unable to discard useful items, though no one comes to claim them, and I frequently misplace my umbrella. I no longer leave footprints in the snow. Because our nation has enjoyed such a prolonged period of domestic peace, I wonder if I still possess my former resilience, though I know I once did. 
> 
> I recall a story about a boy who tied a string to his brother, connecting him to the ocean, and the ocean to a blackbird. Viewed from the ground, every bird appears to be a blackbird, just as a Stealth Bomber can be mistaken for a spaceship. Visitors from another world walk through birthday parties virtually undetected—which is precisely how I navigate my own existence. 
> 
> Having once heated a spoon in the microwave, I am reminded of how modern fish carry enough mercury to spark. I was once presented with a Civil War bayonet and a heavily corroded copper penny. It is said that when the Statue of Liberty is disassembled for restoration, her neck bursts with a million small spiders. Meanwhile, somewhere in a remote forest, someone has opened my grandmother’s abdomen and filled it with bricks. Sensing that an event is imminent, I maintain a bucket of lamb's blood by the front entrance."

### Key Improvements Made:
* **Syntax & Punctuation:** Transformed run-on sentences into balanced, rhythmic statements to improve readability.
* **Elevated Diction:** Replaced casual phrasing (e.g., *"if I still got it"* $\rightarrow$ *"retain my edge/resilience"*, *"basically go unnoticed"* $\rightarrow$ *"virtually unnoticed"*).
* **Narrative Flow:** Added subtle transitional words (*"In much the same way," "Meanwhile"*) to stitch the surreal shifts together seamlessly without altering any original facts or metaphors.
outputs.L2:
Discarding functional belongings proves impossible for me, yet nobody will come to collect them; meanwhile, the location of my rain protection constantly slips my mind. Freshly fallen snow no longer retains my tracks. Because such an extensive period has elapsed without conflict on home soil, I doubt whether my old edge remains, though I definitely possessed it at one time. 

A story reached me about a child who bound his brother with twine, tethered his sibling to the sea, and linked the sea to a blackbird. Viewed from ground level, every avian creature resembles a blackbird, just as a radar-evading military aircraft looks like an extraterrestrial vessel. Earth is being visited by aliens, who stroll through birthday celebrations almost entirely undetected—a subtle style of movement that reflects my own path through existence. 

On one occasion, I placed a metal eating utensil inside a microwave; nowadays, aquatic life is so saturated with mercury that it generates sparks. Someone presented me with a blade from the American Civil War alongside a heavily oxidized copper cent. Whenever the Statue of Liberty is dismantled for maintenance, a million tiny arachnids erupt from her throat. Meanwhile, hidden deep within a woodland, an individual sliced open my grandmother's abdomen and stuffed it full of masonry blocks. Something approaches shortly, which is why a pail of young sheep's blood sits beside my entrance.
outputs.L3:
A profound sense of alienation haunts my waking hours, casting me as a stranger in a world I no longer understand. As I move through the mundane rhythms of everyday life, I feel completely unnoticed, drifting through crowds like an alien who has somehow wandered into a child’s birthday party—present, yet utterly detached from the joy and language of everyone around me. Compounding this isolation is the slow, relentless erosion of time. Aging and a fading memory have begun to blur my history, leaving me to anxiously question whether I still retain the physical strength or combat readiness that once defined my younger years, or if those instincts have withered away entirely.

This internal rust mirrors the surreal, decaying world outside my window. We inhabit a landscape choked by extreme pollution, a toxic environment where nature itself has been grotesquely altered. Down in the dead rivers, heavy mercury contamination has saturated the wildlife to such a degree that the fish spark and glint with a sharp, unnatural luminescence beneath the murky surface. 

Even the sky offers no refuge of clarity, as distance and shifting perspectives warp my view of reality. When military stealth bombers cut silently through the upper atmosphere, their sharp, geometric forms look less like human weaponry and more like alien spaceships hovering on the edge of the cosmos, confusing terror with sci-fi abstraction.

Driven by a mounting anxiety over an unseen, impending threat—and lacking the confidence in my own strength to fight it—I have surrendered to a desperate, ancient paranoia. Beside my front door, sitting like a grotesque silent sentry, rests a bucket filled with lamb’s blood. It is a primitive, ritualistic shield, kept in the quiet hope that whatever dark force is coming will see the mark and pass me by.
outputs.L4:
How did my mother’s face look under the porch light? Was it 1974, or was it only yesterday? The film of the memory is peeling back at the edges, yellowing like the heavy, metallic water that creeps from the brass taps every morning. They always told us the lead builds up in the bones first. It slumbers in the marrow until you turn sixty, and then it wakes up, thirsty, to drink your name. I forget the word for that gray bird on the fence—the one with the oil-sheen on its wings. Everything carries oil now. The river behind the dead chemical plant doesn't freeze in November anymore; it just thickens into a slow, purple jelly, swallowing rusted tires, plastic bottles, and the bloated, pale bellies of dead carp. My hands tremble as I try to turn the radio dial, not just from the palsy, but because the air smells perpetually of scorched copper and sulfur. 

In the attic, buried under damp quilts, my grandfather’s bayonet still smells of gun grease and cold iron. I run my thumb along the notch carved into the oak handle—three shallow cuts. Did he make them in the mud of Passchendaele while the sky turned to mustard gas, or did he do it decades later, sitting alone in the cellar while grandmother wept into her apron? The mud never leaves the wool. Even now, if I press my ear to the tarnished daguerreotype of the boy in the high-collared coat, I don't hear silence; I hear the rhythmic, hollow *thud-thud-thud* of distant 105s. Or perhaps that is just the erratic pounding of my own failing carotid artery. A wet, desperate rhythm. The boy’s eyes in the photograph are black silver-nitrate voids. He knows what came out of the dark woods back then. The old folks in the valley used to say that if you buried an iron nail under the threshold, the Strangler wouldn't cross. But what if the Strangler is already in the well? What if he’s in the grey ash falling softly from the burning forests three hundred miles away?

The crows know. They cluster on the cell towers—monsters of lattice steel rusted red like dried arterial blood—and they speak in the voices of drowned girls. *Three turns of the salt, three turns of the thread.* I dug my fingers into the garden soil under the hydrangeas this morning, but it is dead, ash-dry, woven through with invisible filaments of plastic. Nothing grows right anymore. The tomatoes came up bruised and misshapen, like swollen, severed thumbs. They are watching from the tree line. I can hear a low, hummed frequency vibrating behind the wallpaper, settling deep into the mercury fillings of my teeth. Is it the government’s array on the ridge, or is it the earth’s final, exhausted shudder before the continental shelf snaps? 

I locked the oak door, but the rot doesn't need a key. It seeps under the floorboards, smelling of peat and ancient, unburied bone—like that bog body they dragged from the black moss when I was a boy. Its skin was cured into dark leather, its mouth frozen in a permanent, silent shriek that has been traveling through the atmosphere for a thousand years, finally settling here, in my cold kitchen.

I am leaking away, minute by minute. Names, dates, the scent of rain on pine, the shape of my first dog, the exact shade of my wife’s eyes before the white fog of dementia swallowed her—all of it pouring out into the dust beneath my feet. The world outside the window is dying in reverse, unspooling into smoke and cinder. The horizon wears an angry, bruised orange glow that never fully darkens into night. War in the east, poison in the rain, fire in the north, and a bitter, chemical dryness on my tongue. The radio offers only static now, but if you listen close—between the white noise and the crackle of cosmic radiation—a calm, mechanical voice is counting down from a number I am no longer smart enough to comprehend. I am an old man trapped in a house of fading relics that will soon belong to no one. The sky grows heavy, bruised and low, ready to drop its iron ceiling, and I cannot remember how to pray—only the old dark rhyme about the crow that ate the sun, leaving us all to freeze alone in the dark.
outputs.L5:
Deep in the midnight black of the upper atmosphere, the aircraft glided like a phantom silhouette against the stars. It was a modern marvel of engineering—a high-altitude **stealth bomber** designed to render the vast, complex networks of enemy air defenses utterly obsolete.

Inside the pressurized cockpit, the two pilots sat in near-total silence, bathed in the faint green glow of their instrument panels. No radio chatter was permitted. This was not **because** they lacked things to say, but **because** even a single stray electronic emission could slice through the darkness, giving ground-based tracking systems the tiny clue they needed to lock on. 

Below them lay thousands of square miles of hostile territory, heavily guarded by state-of-the-art radar grids. Yet to those sweeping electronic eyes, the massive flying wing registered as nothing more than a passing breeze or a tiny migratory bird. The craft’s radar-absorbent skin and angled geometry defied detection, allowing it to slip through the sky unnoticed.

Tension mounted as they reached the primary target zone. **Because** the element of surprise was their greatest weapon, the execution had to be flawless. With a quiet chime from the navigation computer, the belly of the plane opened. The weapons bay doors parted for just a few seconds—a brief, calculated risk that temporarily disrupted the aircraft's **stealth** profile.

A single precision payload dropped, disappearing into the dark abyss toward the facility far below. 

Instantly, the bay doors sealed shut again, restoring the seamless, radar-evading shape of the aircraft. Down on the ground, the impact would be devastating, but by the time the smoke began to rise, the sky above would already be empty. The **stealth bomber** banked smoothly toward the ocean, vanishing into the horizon simply **because** it had mastered the rare art of becoming invisible in plain sight.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a surreal stream-of-consciousness prose poem that weaves together themes of aging, paranoia, strange urban legends, and fragmented memories.
counterfactuals.output:
The bathroom mirror is a slow, silver lake where my reflection arrives three seconds late, pulling a gray hair that turns into an insulated copper wire between my thumb and forefinger, my knuckles clicking like an old telegraph sending *S-O-S* to a navy that sank in 1973. Did you hear about the woman who swallowed her own shadow at the 24-hour laundromat on 4th? She paid with wooden tokens that smelled of river mud, and now the streetlamps outside my window dim in the exact rhythm of my arrhythmic pulse, breathing, watching, taking notes on yellow legal pads. My skin is getting so thin I can see the blueprints of the house I grew up in traced in purple veins across my wrists, but the front door is missing and the wallpaper is stained with maraschino cherry juice—or was it the blood from the boy who stuck his tongue to the freezer coils and became part of the appliance? 

The radio on the nightstand only plays the static between stations, but if you listen close enough, beneath the white noise, it’s broadcasting the names of everyone who ever crossed the grid-locked bridge after midnight and never arrived on the other side. They say if you step on a crack, the sewer alligator doesn’t break your mother’s back, it just takes a Polaroid of your face and mails it to a vacant lot in Detroit. 

I was six years old once, wearing a yellow raincoat that smelled of salt, holding a tin cup, or maybe I was seventy-two, sitting on a velvet couch while the walls sweated lead paint. The calendar in the kitchen has thirteen months and all the Tuesdays are gouged out with a rusty key. 

Listen. The floorboards are humming. The neighbors upstairs are swapping their faces again; I can hear the soft *rip-click* of velcro in the dark, exchanging crow’s feet for smoothness, exchanging memories of a childhood in Maine for a drowning in a flooded quarry that hasn't happened yet. They know I know. They put microscopic silver fish in the municipal water line—I read it on a mimeographed pamphlet stuck to the belly of a dead pigeon—and now every time I drink, my eyes forget the word for *ellipse*, the word for *daughter*, the word for *home*. 

The hallway keeps getting longer, stretching like warm saltwater taffy toward a door that wasn't there when I moved in, a door with a peephole that looks inward, showing me a room filled with my own discarded teeth, glowing like chalk under a blacklight. Don't answer the phone if it rings three times and drops to a low frequency hum. That’s just the city trying to trace your bone density. I am shrinking into an origami crane made of unread junk mail, drifting down the elevator shaft where the phantom conductor sweeps up the dust of old birthdays, waiting for the red light at the end of the line to finally, mercifully, turn green.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft an inner monologue for an eccentric narrator who feels invisible in modern society. Use bizarre non-sequiturs, dark folklore, and apocalyptic imagery.
counterfactuals.output:
The man in the tailored houndstooth coat just walked right through the space where my spleen should be. Or perhaps his shoulder merely clipped my coat, but the effect is the same: I am an illusion woven from stale exhaust and old receipts. He didn’t look up from his glowing glass rectangle. Nobody does. To them, I am a gap between seconds, a breath of air that forgot to contain oxygen. 

Do they know the Leshy takes the soles of your boots if you step over a fallen pine with your coat buttoned wrong? Of course not. They think shoes come from Amazon. They don't know about the forest. They don't know that mustard is just angry sunshine.

*Beep. Beep. Beep.* The crosswalk signal is chirping again. It’s trying to warn the pigeons about the price of butter in 1842, but the pigeons are too busy eating a discarded wrapper. Fools. All of them. 

I standing on the corner of 5th and Main, drowning in a sea of beige trench coats and noise-canceling headphones, completely, gloriously erased. I waved my hand in front of a woman pushing a stroller—a double-decker plastic spaceship—and she didn’t even blink. Her eyes skipped over me like a flat stone over a dead lake. I am a changeling left in a steel crib, fed on zinc and Wi-Fi, grown up into a ghost who still pays taxes. 

If I screamed, it would sound like a dry leaf rattling in an air duct.

Look at these glass towers. They build them slick and tall, thinking the ancient things can't scale smooth surfaces. Arrogant swine! The Strigoi don't use the stairs; they ride the 5G waves straight into the ears of the middle management. I saw one yesterday, slithering down an email chain, smelling of wet earth and copper. I tried to point it out to the barista, but he just asked if I wanted oat milk or almond milk. 

I wanted salt. I wanted to scatter salt across the threshold of the bank so the blood-brokers couldn't get back to their desks.

The sky today is a bruised lung, waiting for the final gasp. Soon, the concrete will remember it was once mountains, and it will shudder. It will shake off these glass ticks. The sun will curdle into a yolk of black grease, sliding down the dome of the firmament, and Wormwood will burst from the fire hydrants! Rivers of molten iron will sweep away the pop-up shops! The Seven-Headed Beast will demand to see everyone's transit pass! 

And when the Black Sow comes to reap the untethered souls, she will look right through me, too. 

"Too thin," she’ll snort, her breath smelling of rot and fallen acorns. "Too much bog-oak in his marrow. Not enough blue light."

A cyclist swoops past, missing my hip by an inch. He smells of synthetic rain and panic. He didn't see me. The wind of his passing turns my tie over my shoulder. I am a ghost clinging to a burning planet, waiting for the ash to settle so I can finally sit down.

I should buy a turnip. The turnip remembers the shovel, even when the soil forgets the rain. 

The light turns green. The tide of humanity surges forward, a stampede of polite, distracted cattle marching toward the end of days. I step into the crowd, completely weightless, a tear in the fabric of the morning rush hour. I split their ranks like a rusty knife through cold tallow, and not a single one of them bleeds.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a short, uncanny piece of flash fiction combining mundane modern observations—like forgetting an umbrella or microwaving metal—with intense surrealism and historical violence.
counterfactuals.output:
Arthur had left the stainless-steel fork in the microwave, a 1000-watt lapse in judgment that immediately began to sing. 

Lightning danced along the prongs—bright, violent blue arcs that smelled less like ozone and more like horse sweat, black powder, and scorching wool. Through the darkened glass of the door, his bowl of leftover rigatoni was no longer turning. In its place, tiny, three-inch cavalrymen in mud-caked uniforms from the Battle of Waterloo were trampling one another over the glass turntable. A miniaturized bronze cannon flashed, blowing off the microwave’s door latch with a delicate, muffled *thump*. 

Arthur sighed. He was going to be late for his quarterly review. 

He reached for his jacket, only to remember he had left his umbrella in the backseat of his Hyundai. *Typical*, he thought, stepping out of his apartment into the carpeted hallway. 

It wasn't raining water outside the window at the end of the hall; it was raining the Siege of Magdeburg. Heavy, iron-tipped bolts and severed fingers fell from the grey sky, clinking rhythmically against the exterior air conditioning units. The beige wallpaper peeled back to reveal thick layers of crushed limestone and ancient, calcified ribs, vibrating softly with the low hum of bad Wi-Fi.

Mrs. Gable opened her door across the hall, holding her leash. At the end of it was not her usual cockapoo, but a tangled knot of rusted French bayonets and writhing trench-rats from 1916, barking cheerfully.

"Did you put metal in the appliance again, Arthur?" she asked. Her teeth were ground down to smooth, ivory flints, dripping lukewarm marinara. 

"Just the fork," Arthur said, pressing his thumb against his temple to stave off a migraine. "And I forgot my umbrella."

"You always forget," she chided, stepping over a puddle of boiling pitch that had bubbled up through the linoleum. 

A stray, thumb-sized catapult stone burst through the hallway drywall, clipping Arthur’s ear. Blood ran down his collar—bright, hot, and smelling faintly of garlic bread. He pulled a crumpled paper towel from his pocket to dab at it, thoroughly annoyed that he’d have to change his shirt before catching the 8:15 bus, which was currently being dragged down the avenue by twelve blinded Roman captives in heavy wooden yokes.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a prose poem in the style of contemporary surrealism, starting with everyday clutter and escalating into an apocalyptic fever dream.
counterfactuals.output: It starts in the third drawer down: four dead AAA batteries, a plastic bread tag shaped like a broken tooth, and three yards of thermal receipts weeping faint, purple ink onto a tangle of rusted keys. By midnight, the keys are learning to bloom. They sprout serrated, brass buds that hum with the low frequency of an idle refrigerator. In the corner, the mountain of unfolded laundry begins to breathe in slow, cotton-heavy lungfuls, swallowing the dust mites and spitting back small, wet origami birds that smell of lavender detergent and ozone. You reach to turn off the desk lamp, but the switch clicks into an unfamiliar third position—*future*—and the room turns the color of curdled milk. Outside, the streetlights drop their heads like sunburnt lilies, bleeding warm sodium light onto the lawn until the grass hardens into black glass. The sky does not fall; it simply unspools like a magnetic tape, a dark ribbon tangling in the telephone wires, broadcasting millions of automated voicemails simultaneously. The neighbors' houses lose their corners, melting down into smooth, beige incisors rooted in the asphalt. The horizon folds itself in half with the dry snap of a cardboard box. In the distance, the ocean boils down to a thick syrup of plastic spools and iridescent jellyfish, while the moon flickers, revealing itself to be nothing more than the unblinking, backlit logo of a 24-hour gas station floating in the void. Then comes the rain—not water, but a heavy, silent deluge of plastic pull-tabs and crushed copper wire that buries the sedans up to their side-view mirrors. You stand on your balcony, wrapped in a blanket woven from discarded user manuals, watching the sun get swallowed by a giant, floating pair of rusted scissors. You reach into your pocket for a coin, a match, anything to anchor the room, but your fingers find only a faded coupon, long expired, offering ten percent off a world that was never yours to keep.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Give me a creative writing piece incorporating these elements: a stealth bomber mistaken for an alien spaceship, spiders inside the Statue of Liberty, a fairy tale reference about bricks in a grandmother's belly, and a bucket of lamb's blood by the front door.
counterfactuals.output:
The wind off the New York harbor carried the bitter tang of salt and cold iron, but on Arthur’s porch, a different scent prevailed: thick, metallic, and warm. 

By the front door sat a galvanized steel bucket filled to the brim with fresh lamb’s blood. Arthur dipped a thick horsehair brush into the crimson pool and painted a heavy, glistening line across the threshold. He didn’t care if the neighbors on the Jersey shore thought he was mad. Old world habits die hard, especially when the end of the world arrives in whispers.

He looked up at the night sky. 

It was happening again. High above the low-hanging clouds, a shape sliced through the stars. It possessed no flashing navigational lights, emitted no thundering roar of jet fuel, and defied the familiar curves of human architecture. It was a perfect, matte-black wedge—a tear in the geometry of the heavens. 

Arthur held his breath, his knuckles white against the wooden porch railing. The conspiracy channels on the shortwave radio were calling it *The Overseer*, convinced it was an extraterrestrial dreadnought scouting Earth's defenses before the harvest. Arthur couldn't blame them; the weaponized ghost glided with impossible, eerie silence. He didn't know that three hundred miles south, in a soundproof bunker, air force engineers were monitoring the radar-evading radar signatures of a secret prototype stealth bomber. To Arthur, standing in the dark, it was simply an alien beast floating above a doomed world.

His gaze drifted from the flying shadow down to the waters of the harbor, where the Statue of Liberty stood silhouetted against the Manhattan glow. 

Arthur knew a secret about the Lady. For twenty years, he had been part of the night maintenance crew, climbing the dizzying, spiral staircases deep within her hollow bronze skirt. Visitors thought of her as a beacon of light, but inside, she was a humid, iron-ribbed tomb. And in that dark, undisturbed interior, tens of thousands of yellow garden spiders and brown recluses had made a home. 

They spun endless, thick curtains of silk across Gustave Eiffel’s steel armature, swaying gently in the drafts that snaked up from the river. Millions of tiny, jointed legs scurried over the rivets in the dark. The grand symbol of freedom was, from the inside out, completely infested—a hollow idol held together by spiderwebs and shadows.

Arthur shivered, pulling his woolen coat tighter around his chest. The heavy, suffocating feeling in the air reminded him of his grandmother. 

When he was a boy in the mountains, she used to sit by the hearth and tell him the unedited, brutal versions of ancient fairy tales. Her favorite was the story of the dark forest beast—the one who swallowed grandmothers whole. But in her telling, the story didn't end with a heroic woodsman. 

*"The old woman didn't die in the beast's stomach, little one,"* she would whisper, her hands rough as bark against his cheek. *"She sat in the dark inside its gut, and brick by red brick, she built a furnace in its belly. She filled the creature up with heavy stone and mortar until it was too burdened to run, too heavy to hunt, until its own stolen weight tore it open from the inside."*

Arthur felt that same heavy, brick-like weight dragging in his own stomach now. The world felt stuffed with heavy things—secret bombers posing as alien gods, statues hollowed out by millions of venomous spinners, ancient fears demanding blood at the door. 

Above the harbor, the stealth bomber angled its sharp, triangular wing and vanished into a thick bank of fog, silent as a thought. Out in the water, Lady Liberty stood motionless, her iron ribs cradling a dark, writhing army of silk and legs.

Arthur lowered his brush back into the bucket of lamb's blood. He turned the lock on his door, stepped inside, and waited for the night to break its teeth against his doorstep.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
